screens.title: Scripting and Executing Administrative Commands
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll make T-S Q L your dependable, auditable tool for administrative work. You will learn how to create and map logins and users, inspect database settings, and script common tasks so they run the same way every time. We'll introduce dynamic S Q L as a way to write flexible scripts that adapt to your schema, while also showing how to avoid security pitfalls like S Q L injection through proper parameterization and least-privilege design. By the end, you'll be comfortable reading system views to discover objects and permissions, creating password or Azure AD users appropriately, and building safe, repeatable maintenance scripts. For example, you'll see how to create a login in the master database, then create a mapped user in an application database and grant just the SELECT and INSERT permissions needed — not full ownership. This matters because scripted operations scale, are auditable, and reduce human error during maintenance and deployment. Consider a case where a reporting app needs only read access; scripting that precise permission ensures security and operational consistency. Are you ready to turn one-off admin steps into reliable, testable scripts?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Scripting and Executing Administrative Commands
Scripting and Executing Administrative Commands
Use T-SQL to automate user management, configuration, schema discovery, and safe dynamic execution.
In this lesson

Create logins and users, read system views, and run parameterized dynamic SQL to automate administration.

Why it matters

Scripts are repeatable and auditable. They reduce risk and help enforce least-privilege across environments.

Explore Key Topics
Users & Logins
Differentiate server logins and database users and map them correctly.
Dynamic SQL
Build flexible scripts with sp_executesql and parameterization to avoid injections.
System Views
Query sys.tables, sys.databases, and sys.database_principals for discovery and audits.
Visual overview
Cards show the three pillars: access, settings, and discovery.
Access
Logins and users, mapped correctly, minimize blast radius for credentials.
Configuration
ALTER DATABASE and system views let you inspect and tweak options safely.
Discovery
System views give metadata for auditing and scripted maintenance.
Key Takeaway

Use T-SQL scripts and system views to make administrative work repeatable, auditable, and secure.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the practical skills you'll build. First, you will master T-S Q L scripting for common administrative operations: creating logins and users, granting permissions, and enumerating objects. That means you can produce reliable scripts that are repeatable and auditable across environments. Second, you will understand dynamic S Q L—how to build statements at runtime for flexibility and how to avoid unsafe patterns. We'll show examples of sp_executesql and parameter usage so you can write flexible scripts without opening injection vulnerabilities. Each objective ties to real tasks you perform as an Azure DBA, like provisioning a reporting user or changing a database compatibility level. As you progress, focus on writing scripts that are clear, parameterized, and easily reviewed. These are not just commands you type once; they become part of your operational toolkit that other team members can run safely. A misconception to avoid is thinking dynamic equals insecure; when designed with parameters and least privilege, dynamic scripts are powerful and safe. Keep that tradeoff in mind as you build and test scripts.

screens.title: How we will practice
screens.narratorSegment: You'll practice by writing scripts that you can run and review. Start by creating a login and a mapped database user, then grant the exact permissions required by the application. Next, build a small dynamic script to list or act upon multiple objects — for example, granting SELECT across all tables in a schema — and convert it to use sp_executesql with parameters. To verify your work, query system views to confirm users, roles, and permissions are present and correct. A common pitfall is assigning too many privileges, so test with an impersonation step or permission query to validate effective permissions. Testing and verification make scripts trustworthy and repeatable for teams. By practicing these verification steps, you bridge the gap between one-off commands and operational automation. Keep test accounts, use parameterization, and ensure scripts are readable and auditable for future administrators.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › How we will practice
Practice checklist
Follow these steps and verify each result with system views.
Provision
Create login and user mapped to that login or an Azure AD identity.
Grant
Grant only required permissions, e.g., SELECT, INSERT on specific tables.
Verify
Query sys.database_principals and sys.database_permissions to confirm outcomes.
Common Mistake

Assigning high-privilege roles like db_owner when granular permissions would suffice increases attack surface and hinders audits.

Pro Tip

Prefer Azure AD identities for managed services and use password-based users only when necessary for compatibility.

screens.title: T-SQL for Administrative Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: Administrative T-S Q L means using the same language you use for data to also manage your environment: create logins and users, change database options, and query system metadata. The benefit is consistency — the commands are repeatable, can be stored in source control, and produce an audit trail. For example, a script that creates a login, creates a mapped user in a database, and grants SELECT on a schema can be rerun against staging and production to produce the same outcome. A common misconception is thinking ad-hoc GUI actions are safer; in reality, scripted steps are clearer to review and reduce manual errors. In practice, administrative scripts should include checks — verify the login doesn't already exist, check the database context, and log results. Use system views such as sys. databases and sys. database_principals to query the current state before making changes. When you wrap administrative steps in scripts, you also make them automatable via deployment pipelines. Consider how automated deployments benefit from idempotent scripts that can be run multiple times without harmful side effects. As you build scripts, include clear comments, parameterize values like database names, and test against a non-production copy first. What one administrative script can you turn into a repeatable, reviewed artifact today?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › T-SQL for Administrative Tasks
What this term means

Administrative T-SQL uses standard SQL commands and system views to perform management work in a repeatable, auditable way.

Why repeatability matters
Scripts can be stored, reviewed, and executed consistently across environments.
Auditability
Commands and outputs can be logged and compared for compliance and incident response.
Practical checks
Scripts should check for existing objects and confirm success before proceeding.
Key Takeaway

Turn one-off admin steps into idempotent scripts that you can test and review.

Example
A scripted flow: verify database exists → create login if missing → create user mapped to login → grant minimal permissions.
-- Conceptual script fragment (illustrative)
-- Check database and create a login + user mapping
USE master;
GO
-- Ensure login exists, then switch to app DB
-- CREATE LOGIN AppLogin WITH PASSWORD = 'YourStrongPassword123!';
-- USE YourApplicationDB; CREATE USER AppUser FOR LOGIN AppLogin;
-- Grant minimal permissions needed by the application
-- GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::dbo TO AppUser;
Misconception
Using GUI steps is always easier. In practice, scripts scale and can be peer-reviewed.
Question
Which administrative step in your workflow should be scripted first, and why?

screens.title: Logins vs Users
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent point of confusion is the relationship between logins and users. A login is a server- or instance-level principal used for authentication. In Azure S Q L Managed Instance and S Q L Server, you create logins at the server level, or within the master database for managed Azure S Q L DB. A user, by contrast, exists inside a specific database and is mapped to a login or an external identity. The distinction matters during provisioning: create the login first so it can authenticate, then create the user in the target database to grant object-level permissions. A concrete example: you would create AppLogin as a server-level login with a strong password and then create AppUser in YourApplicationDB mapped to AppLogin, granting SELECT and INSERT on the tables the application needs. A common mistake is granting broad roles like db_owner because it is faster; that violates the principle of least privilege. When using Azure AD, you can create users directly from the external provider and avoid password management. Before deployment, verify mappings by querying sys. server_principals and sys. database_principals and confirm user mapping entries. What mapping checks will you add to your script to avoid orphaned users?

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Logins authenticate at the server level; users authorize access within a database and are mapped to logins or external identities.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Logins vs Users
Login (Server Principal)
Authenticates to the server
  • - Created at server or in master for Azure SQL DB
  • - Example: CREATE LOGIN AppLogin WITH PASSWORD = '...'
  • - Controls who can open a connection
Verification
Query sys.server_principals to confirm the login exists and attributes like authentication type.
User (Database Principal)
Authorizes access within a database
  • - Created inside each database and mapped to a login or external provider
  • - Example: CREATE USER AppUser FOR LOGIN AppLogin
  • - Grants permissions on objects in that database
Verification
Query sys.database_principals and sys.database_role_members to inspect membership and roles.
Concrete example
Create login in master. Create user in application DB mapped to login. Grant minimal privileges.
Prefer Azure AD users where possible to centralize identity management.
Avoid db_owner; grant schema or object-level permissions instead.

screens.title: Create a Login and Mapped User
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete script for creating a login and a mapped user. This example applies to Azure S Q L Managed Instance or S Q L Server on a VM. The steps are: switch to the master database, create the login with a strong password and recommended checks, then switch to the application database and create a user mapped to that login. Finally grant only the rights the application requires, such as SELECT and INSERT on specific objects. When you run these commands, ensure the password meets your organization's complexity rules and that you run this from an account that has permission to create logins. A common misconception is that passwords can be hard-coded into shared scripts; instead, store sensitive values securely and parameterize scripts for deployment. After creation, verify the objects using sys. server_principals and sys. database_principals and confirm the grants via sys. database_permissions. This pattern yields a reproducible provisioning step you can incorporate into automation pipelines or run manually with clear rollback plans. Create a Login and Mapped User means create the login in the server context, create the user in the database context, grant minimal object permissions, and verify with system views.. In practical terms, practical t-sql examples for provisioned access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create the login in the server context, create the user in the database context, grant minimal object permissions, and verify with system views.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Create a Login and Mapped User
T-SQL Example
USE master; -- Or the master DB for Azure SQL DB
GO

CREATE LOGIN AppLogin WITH PASSWORD = 'YourStrongPassword123!', CHECK_POLICY = ON;
GO

USE YourApplicationDB; -- Replace with actual DB name
GO

CREATE USER AppUser FOR LOGIN AppLogin;
GO

-- Grant specific permissions
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::dbo TO AppUser;
GRANT INSERT ON dbo.Orders TO AppUser;
GO
Example intent
Create application credentials that map authentication to database authorization.
Misconception
Don't give db_owner to simplify permissions; assign minimal object rights instead.
Verification steps
  • Query sys.server_principals to see the created login.
  • Use sys.database_principals to confirm the database user exists and is mapped.
  • Check sys.database_permissions to confirm grants are applied.
Key Takeaway

Always verify created principals and permissions with system views after running provisioning scripts.

screens.title: Azure AD Users and External Provider
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Active Directory integration simplifies credential management for Azure S Q L. Rather than creating S Q L logins with passwords, you can provision database users from the external provider, which uses centralized identities and avoids storing database passwords in scripts. The T-S Q L form is CREATE USER with FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER, and you can target groups or individual AAD principals. A concrete use case is granting an App Service managed identity access: create a database user for that identity and grant only the needed permissions. This reduces operational overhead for credential rotation and makes access revocation easier through Azure AD. A misconception is that external users reduce the need for careful permission design; they do not. You still must apply least privilege. When scripting these steps, document the required Azure AD object names and confirm that the managed identity or group exists in the tenant before running the S Q L. After creation, verify membership and effective permissions using system views to ensure expected access. How will you adopt AD-based identities in your environment to simplify credential lifecycle?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Azure AD Users and External Provider
Example: Create an Azure AD user
Use CREATE USER [AAD_User_Name] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER; for individuals, or CREATE USER [AAD_Group_Name] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER; for groups.
Benefits
Centralizes identity, simplifies credential rotation, and integrates with enterprise access controls.
Checklist before creating
Confirm tenant membership and object names, and ensure necessary Azure roles are assigned externally.
Practical note
Prefer AD identities for managed services, and document the mapping in your deployment runbook.
Common Mistake

Assuming AD users eliminate the need for permission reviews; continue to apply least privilege and verify effective access.

screens.title: Granting Permissions and Least Privilege
screens.narratorSegment: Granting permissions is a three-step process: decide the minimal privilege, apply the grant to the precise object or schema, and verify effective access. Start by choosing the narrowest permission—schema-level SELECT may suffice rather than table-level grants, and object-level rights are preferred over fixed roles like db_owner. For example, if an application only needs to read and insert into Orders and Customers, grant SELECT on the dbo schema and INSERT on dbo. Orders rather than adding the user to a broad role. After granting, verify using sys. database_permissions and simulate access if possible by impersonating the user or querying HAS_PERMS_BY_NAME for specific objects. A common misconception is that role-based assignments are always safer; roles are useful for grouping rights but must still follow least privilege. When scripting grants, use idempotent checks to avoid duplicate grants and include a verification query at the end to produce an auditable result. This discipline reduces attack surface and makes it easier to revoke or adjust access later. Which permission boundaries will you document for each role in your environment? Granting Permissions and Least Privilege means decide minimal privileges, grant only those permissions, and verify effective access with impersonation or permission queries.. In practical terms, grant, verify, and avoid over-privileging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Granting Permissions and Least Privilege
Grant flow
1. Decide minimal privilege
Map application actions to the least set of permissions required.
2. Apply grants precisely
Grant on objects or schemas instead of assigning broad roles.
3. Verify and log
Use system views and permission checks to record effective rights.
Concrete example
Grant SELECT on a schema and INSERT on a specific table to a reporting user. Avoid db_owner assignment.
Key Takeaway

Design grants around actions, not convenience. Automate checks to ensure grants are correct and auditable.

Verification snippet
Query sys.database_permissions joined to sys.database_principals to list permissions granted to a user for auditing.

screens.title: Database Property Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Database properties control behavior and compatibility. You can view options in sys. databases and change many settings with ALTER DATABASE. A practical example is changing compatibility level to match a target engine version: set compatibility level to 150 for S Q L Server 2019 or similar Azure targets. Another administrative action might be inspecting auto-shrink or auto-close settings; auto-shrink is generally discouraged because it can cause fragmentation and unpredictable IO patterns. When executing ALTER DATABASE commands, validate that the change is supported in your environment and test in a non-production copy first. Use queries against sys. databases to collect the current state and make decisions in scripts: for instance, only alter the database if the current compatibility level differs from the desired one. A misconception is thinking configuration changes are instantly risk-free; some changes affect execution plans or storage behavior and must be tested. When scripting, emit an audit record of the previous and new values so changes can be reviewed later. Database Property Configuration means use alter database to change settings and sys.databases to read current values; validate changes before applying.. In practical terms, alter database and querying sys.databases for settings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Database Property Configuration
Examples
-- Change compatibility level
ALTER DATABASE YourApplicationDB
SET COMPATIBILITY_LEVEL = 150; -- Example for SQL Server 2019 / Azure SQL DB

-- View current database options
SELECT name, is_auto_close_on, is_auto_shrink_on, compatibility_level
FROM sys.databases
WHERE name = 'YourApplicationDB';
When scripting such changes, check the current state first and only run ALTER when needed to avoid unnecessary plan changes and to provide a clear audit trail.
Considerations
  • Test compatibility changes in a copy of production to detect plan regressions.
  • Avoid enabling auto-shrink; it can harm performance.
  • Record prior settings for rollback and auditing.
Common Mistake

Applying configuration changes in production without validation can cause unexpected performance differences.

screens.title: Object Enumeration with System Views
screens.narratorSegment: Object enumeration is the practice of querying system views to discover the schema and objects in a database. Common views include sys. tables, sys. views, sys. procedures, and sys. columns. You use these views to audit schema, locate objects for maintenance scripts, or build reports of object counts and dependencies. For example, to create a script that rebuilds indexes or grants permissions across many tables, first query sys. tables joined to sys. schemas to get fully qualified names. A misconception is assuming object names won't change; always script discovery so your maintenance actions adapt to schema updates. System views are efficient and intended for this purpose, but when you use them in dynamic scripts, ensure you quote object names with QUOTENAME to guard against unusual identifiers. Also record the discovery output as part of your run to provide an audit trail for what objects were targeted. How will you include discovery and quoting in your next maintenance script? Object Enumeration with System Views means use sys.* views to programmatically discover objects for audits and scripted maintenance, and protect names with quotename.. screens.title: Dynamic SQL and sp_executesql
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic S Q L is the technique of building T-S Q L statements as strings at runtime and executing them. It adds flexibility when object names or filters vary. The simplest execution uses EXEC, but sp_executesql is preferred because it supports parameterization. Using parameters prevents S Q L injection and improves plan reuse. For instance, build a query string that selects from a schema but pass filter values as parameters to sp_executesql rather than concatenating them into the string. A common misconception is that dynamic S Q L is inherently insecure; it is risky when unparameterized user input is concatenated directly. The mitigation is clear: use sp_executesql with explicit parameter definitions and pass values separately, and always QUOTENAME object names when they come from metadata. Another practical tip is to limit permissions of the executing principal so dynamic scripts cannot escalate beyond intended scope. After writing a dynamic script, test it with representative inputs and compare behavior to static equivalents. If you need to rebuild indexes or grant permissions across many objects, dynamic S Q L lets a single script adapt to schema changes safely when parameterized correctly.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Advanced Dynamic SQL: Rebuild Indexes
Maintenance script example
DECLARE @SchemaName NVARCHAR(128) = N'dbo';
DECLARE @TableName NVARCHAR(256);
DECLARE @IndexRebuildSQL NVARCHAR(MAX);

DECLARE cur_tables CURSOR FOR
SELECT QUOTENAME(s.name) + '.' + QUOTENAME(t.name)
FROM sys.tables t
JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
WHERE s.name = @SchemaName;

OPEN cur_tables;
FETCH NEXT FROM cur_tables INTO @TableName;

WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
BEGIN
    SET @IndexRebuildSQL = N'PRINT ''Rebuilding indexes on ' + @TableName + '''; ' +
                           N'ALTER INDEX ALL ON ' + @TableName + N' REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON);';
    EXEC sp_executesql @IndexRebuildSQL;
    FETCH NEXT FROM cur_tables INTO @TableName;
END;

CLOSE cur_tables;
DEALLOCATE cur_tables;
GO
Notes
  • QUOTENAME prevents issues with special characters in identifiers.
  • Log outputs and PRINT statements to capture progress.
  • Test the ONLINE option and consider maintenance windows.
Caution

Dynamic maintenance can be powerful but must be tested for locking and resource impact before production runs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll make T-S Q L your dependable, auditable tool for administrative work. You will learn how to create and map logins and users, inspect database settings, and script common tasks so they run the same way every time. We'll introduce dynamic S Q L as a way to write flexible scripts that adapt to your schema, while also showing how to avoid security pitfalls like S Q L injection through proper parameterization and least-privilege design. By the end, you'll be comfortable reading system views to discover objects and permissions, creating password or Azure AD users appropriately, and building safe, repeatable maintenance scripts. For example, you'll see how to create a login in the master database, then create a mapped user in an application database and grant just the SELECT and INSERT permissions needed — not full ownership. This matters because scripted operations scale, are auditable, and reduce human error during maintenance and deployment. Consider a case where a reporting app needs only read access; scripting that precise permission ensures security and operational consistency. Are you ready to turn one-off admin steps into reliable, testable scripts?

These objectives guide the practical skills you'll build. First, you will master T-S Q L scripting for common administrative operations: creating logins and users, granting permissions, and enumerating objects. That means you can produce reliable scripts that are repeatable and auditable across environments. Second, you will understand dynamic S Q L—how to build statements at runtime for flexibility and how to avoid unsafe patterns. We'll show examples of sp_executesql and parameter usage so you can write flexible scripts without opening injection vulnerabilities. Each objective ties to real tasks you perform as an Azure DBA, like provisioning a reporting user or changing a database compatibility level. As you progress, focus on writing scripts that are clear, parameterized, and easily reviewed. These are not just commands you type once; they become part of your operational toolkit that other team members can run safely. A misconception to avoid is thinking dynamic equals insecure; when designed with parameters and least privilege, dynamic scripts are powerful and safe. Keep that tradeoff in mind as you build and test scripts.

You'll practice by writing scripts that you can run and review. Start by creating a login and a mapped database user, then grant the exact permissions required by the application. Next, build a small dynamic script to list or act upon multiple objects — for example, granting SELECT across all tables in a schema — and convert it to use sp_executesql with parameters. To verify your work, query system views to confirm users, roles, and permissions are present and correct. A common pitfall is assigning too many privileges, so test with an impersonation step or permission query to validate effective permissions. Testing and verification make scripts trustworthy and repeatable for teams. By practicing these verification steps, you bridge the gap between one-off commands and operational automation. Keep test accounts, use parameterization, and ensure scripts are readable and auditable for future administrators.

Administrative T-S Q L means using the same language you use for data to also manage your environment: create logins and users, change database options, and query system metadata. The benefit is consistency — the commands are repeatable, can be stored in source control, and produce an audit trail. For example, a script that creates a login, creates a mapped user in a database, and grants SELECT on a schema can be rerun against staging and production to produce the same outcome. A common misconception is thinking ad-hoc GUI actions are safer; in reality, scripted steps are clearer to review and reduce manual errors. In practice, administrative scripts should include checks — verify the login doesn't already exist, check the database context, and log results. Use system views such as sys. databases and sys. database_principals to query the current state before making changes. When you wrap administrative steps in scripts, you also make them automatable via deployment pipelines. Consider how automated deployments benefit from idempotent scripts that can be run multiple times without harmful side effects. As you build scripts, include clear comments, parameterize values like database names, and test against a non-production copy first. What one administrative script can you turn into a repeatable, reviewed artifact today?

A frequent point of confusion is the relationship between logins and users. A login is a server- or instance-level principal used for authentication. In Azure S Q L Managed Instance and S Q L Server, you create logins at the server level, or within the master database for managed Azure S Q L DB. A user, by contrast, exists inside a specific database and is mapped to a login or an external identity. The distinction matters during provisioning: create the login first so it can authenticate, then create the user in the target database to grant object-level permissions. A concrete example: you would create AppLogin as a server-level login with a strong password and then create AppUser in YourApplicationDB mapped to AppLogin, granting SELECT and INSERT on the tables the application needs. A common mistake is granting broad roles like db_owner because it is faster; that violates the principle of least privilege. When using Azure AD, you can create users directly from the external provider and avoid password management. Before deployment, verify mappings by querying sys. server_principals and sys. database_principals and confirm user mapping entries. What mapping checks will you add to your script to avoid orphaned users?

Let's walk through a concrete script for creating a login and a mapped user. This example applies to Azure S Q L Managed Instance or S Q L Server on a VM. The steps are: switch to the master database, create the login with a strong password and recommended checks, then switch to the application database and create a user mapped to that login. Finally grant only the rights the application requires, such as SELECT and INSERT on specific objects. When you run these commands, ensure the password meets your organization's complexity rules and that you run this from an account that has permission to create logins. A common misconception is that passwords can be hard-coded into shared scripts; instead, store sensitive values securely and parameterize scripts for deployment. This pattern yields a reproducible provisioning step you can incorporate into automation pipelines or run manually with clear rollback plans. The simplest execution uses EXEC, but sp_executesql is preferred because it supports parameterization. Using parameters prevents S Q L injection and improves plan reuse. For instance, build a query string that selects from a schema but pass filter values as parameters to sp_executesql rather than concatenating them into the string. A common misconception is that dynamic S Q L is inherently insecure; it is risky when unparameterized user input is concatenated directly. The mitigation is clear: use sp_executesql with explicit parameter definitions and pass values separately, and always QUOTENAME object names when they come from metadata. Let's summarize the essential ideas to retain. First, distinguish logins from users: logins authenticate at the server level and users authorize access inside a database. Second, prefer least privilege when granting rights: choose specific object or schema permissions rather than broad roles. Third, use system views like sys. databases, sys. tables, and sys. database_principals for discovery and verification; scripts that query these views are adaptable and auditable. These three concepts form the foundation of secure, scriptable database administration.
